chapter_theme: First songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 1 of 6): the poet confesses his bondage to courtesans who invite, rob and expel, and to the body that rots and dies, imagines the hour of death and Yama's summons, and asks for Murugan's feet; the praise turns on Valli, Vishnu as uncle, Siva and Uma, and the shore of Senthil.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (21, 25 to 27, 29, 32, 33, 35), with 34 showing the same women aged; death songs (23, 28) and the decaying body (30); a love-lament in a mother's voice (24); and 22 and 31, which ask for inner vision and love rather than escape from women.

21.reading: The poet gives the street talk of courtesans who stand at the crossroads pretending to fix their hair: 'Going without love? You came once and never again; what you gave before isn't enough, give today; come to my house', and asks not to fall in vain into these deceitful women's play. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Mayon, who became sky, wind, fire, water, earth, the seven worlds, you, I, Brahma, your Sankara and the gods, yet touches none of them, and the honey known to the hearts of those who live at Senthil.
21.nuance: The first half is reported speech, an unusual dramatic device: the courtesans' words are themselves the confession. In the praise, ஒன்றினும் கடை தோயா மாயோன, Vishnu who becomes everything without being touched by anything, is the pervasion of the Lord, here given to Vishnu as Murugan's uncle. Two words in the second half are garbled.

22.reading: The poet asks when, with Death turned back and the craving for women gone, the three gunas ended, day and night left behind and the senses' agitation cut, singing poems on the lotus feet and knowing Senthil and Kandan ever deeper, his mind will melt and dissolve, his speech end and his own action perish, so that he gains the vision of Murugan. The praise shows Indra crying 'refuge' and regaining his city, Devayanai gaining Murugan's arms, the demons dying, and the child Murugan toddling with bells and anklets ringing until Sankari's heart melts.
22.nuance: The plea moves by repeated doubled words (உணர்ந்துணர்ந்து, அறிந்தறிந்து, அழிந்தழிந்து), as if enacting the deepening it asks for. உரையொழித்து என் செயல் அழிந்து: the end of speech and of one's own agency is the goal, not escape from women alone. The praise ends with Murugan as a toddler (தளர்நடைச் சந்ததி), a tender picture rare in the battle-heavy praise.

23.reading: When the palm-leaf summons of Death, with his fanged and serpent-crowned retinue, arrives, the life faints, drums beat, kin wail, and the body is pushed through the streets; the poet asks whether his heart will not take fright at that departing path and, without the delusion 'this is ours', share even half a kunri seed or a grain of millet, instead of saying 'today, that day'. The praise shows Siva dancing with Uma, the crescent dripping nectar, the matted hair whirling and the drum sounding, and names Murugan the true guru whom that master of dance worships, at Senthil by the sea.
23.nuance: The remedy the plea draws from death is giving, not devotion: குன்றிப் பிளவளவு தினையளவு பங்கிட்டு உண்கை, to eat sharing even a split kunri seed or a millet grain. சமனோலை is Yama's written summons. In the praise Siva the dancer (பரதகுரு) worships Murugan the true guru (சற்குருநாதா).

24.reading: In the voice of a mother, the singer laments that her golden girl, wounded by Kama's lotus arrow, by the anril bird, the south wind and the crescent at evening, has given up all other joy and suffers from love; she asks whether those who bear daughters in this world should meet such a tiger of pleasure. The praise names Murugan the sweet one of the hunter girl, the one who prattled Tamil to explain the one thing to Siva of the konrai-hair, the vel that struck the golden peak, and the lord at Senthil dear to poets of fine speech.
24.nuance: This is akam poetry, a foster-mother's or mother's lament for a girl in love with the god, and there is no confession of the poet's own. The machinery is classical: the paired anril bird, the south wind, the crescent at dusk. கொன்றைச் சடையற்கு ஒன்றைத் தெரியக் கொஞ்சித் தமிழைப் பகர்வோனே: Murugan explains 'the one' to Siva in Tamil, again the teaching of 6 and 12.

25.reading: The poet describes the bejewelled, musk-scented women in whose play he bathed as if in ritual, their hair loosened and ornaments slipping in the dark, and asks that, no longer deluded night and day, he be given fine words in his heart to sing Murugan's paired feet and live. The praise names Siva of the serpent and matted hair, source of the four Vedas, and Vishnu, the cloud-hued one who answered the elephant that first thought of him crying 'Root!', and calls Murugan the victorious Saravana whose vel pierced Sura's chest and the hill, at Senthil.
25.nuance: அபிஷேக மீதென: the poet calls his bathing in women's play an abhisheka, a sacred bath, an irony. The plea is for the gift of song (செஞ்சொல்), as in 2. The elephant crying மூலமே is the story of Gajendra. The lines on Vishnu gathering up the sea-girt earth and sharing nectar with the gods are hard to divide.

26.reading: The poet asks that he not end in the false play of embraces with women whose ear-ornaments wound like spears, and that, with birth ended, he think in his heart on the kadamba-adorned, anklet-bearing feet; he asks Murugan to look with love on the sorrow of one whose love and understanding have gone. The praise calls him the true guru who wondrously showed the form of Siva to the one who conquered with fire the Kama whose flower arrows frightened even ascetics, and the lord of Senthil where the sea casts conch-pearls and the sun's chariot stumbles.
26.nuance: The praise appears to tell of Siva burning Kama (தழலெழ வென்றார்) and of Murugan showing Siva his own form (சிவவடிவம் காட்டும் சற்குருபர); the phrases in between (தென்காற் கன்றில் திரிதரு கஞ்சாக் கன்று) are obscure and the reading is tentative.

27.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women, hair loosened, faces sweating, nails and lips, and asks that, seeing clearly how to leave that embrace, he be given the cool lotus feet with anklets that those of Sivayoga who melt in jnana contemplate. The praise names Siva, son-giver, who drank the poison when Brahma, Vishnu the father of Kama, Indra and the gods cried 'Hara Hara Siva Sankara', and Vishnu who churned the sea as Murugan's uncle, at Senthil, a town of plantain, turmeric and ginger.
27.nuance: சிவயோகத்து உருகு ஞான பரம்பர தந்திர அறிவினோர்: the feet are those that yogis and jnanis hold in mind, so the plea sets the yoga of Siva against the embrace. இரதி வேள் பணி தந்தை is Vishnu, father of Kama (Rati's lord).

28.reading: The poet asks that Death, like fire, not call him while his mind fails, delusion grows, speech goes, eyes roll, the body's fire dies and its filth flows, and his mother and kin weep in fear by the bed; and that, with the two deeds, the instruments and the senses gone, he be given the boon of drawing near the high feet. The praise names Murugan the one who spoke sweet Tamil to delight the sage of Pothiyai, equal to Siva, the vel thrown at Nirudan whose rule harried the sun, moon, Yama, Indra, Agni, Nirruti, Kubera, Vishnu and Brahma, and the child who grew in the laps of Siva and Uma, at the shore of Senthil.
28.nuance: The death is told from the body outward, eyes rolling and filth flowing, then to the weeping mother at the bedside. இருவினை கரணம் மருவுபுலன் ஒழிய names what must fall away. பொதியவரை முநிவன் is Agastya, whom Murugan taught Tamil.

29.reading: The poet speaks of the tender-footed women with gem-set breasts and calls himself the sinner who presses his face to them, a wretch of deeds, an insulted fool who saw great wealth, a ruin who loves flesh, a deluded man who does not walk in dharma, and asks whether he will gain grace if Murugan calls him and gives him his sandals. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea and cut Ravana's heads with one arrow as his uncle, Siva who wears the moon, the serpent, Ganga and flowers as his father, and Murugan as Valli's lover, the champion at Thiruchendur.
29.nuance: The heap of self-abuse (வினைச் சண்டாளன், வீணன், நிர்மூடன், பாழன், மோக விகாரன், மூதேவி) is a set feature of the book. உன் பாதுகை நீ தர, 'that you give your sandals', recalls Rama's sandals, given just before in the praise. விடக்கு அன்பாய் நுகர் may mean loving to eat flesh, or the flesh of the body enjoyed in lust.

30.reading: The poet speaks of carrying this wretched body, which stinks like a corpse, rots in disease, splits and rattles with worms and bones, while all who see it flee and Death follows behind, and of going from house to house speaking sweetly and eating whatever feast comes; he asks when, freed from that disgrace and knowing the four Vedas, he will bow at the flower feet with tinkling bells. The praise names the girl guarding the millet who chased away parrots, Murugan who circled the whole world on his golden peacock before the elephant-faced one and his father, and who told the frightened gods not to fear.
30.nuance: பிணநாறும் அழுகு பிணி ... புழுவுடன் எலும்பு அலம்பும் அவல உடல்: the body is already a corpse while alive. ஜெகமுழுது ... திகிரி வலம் வந்த is the circling of the world in the contest for the fruit (see 3).

31.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to tire himself and wander thinking night and day over a fitting woman praised in poetry and song, but to bathe in the sea of bliss of Murugan's high compassion and be given the love that knows him within. The praise names Murugan who bowed to and embraced the hunter girl guarding the millet field, the life of Senthil that is like Kailasa, the younger brother of the elephant-faced one.
31.nuance: உனை எனதுள் அறியும் அன்பு: the love asked for is one that knows the Lord inside the self. இயலிசையில் உசித வஞ்சி may also mean the deceit of poetry and song, so whether the first line speaks of a woman or of art is uncertain.

32.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women whose eyes dart to their earrings and whose breasts are scented with sandal and kumkum, and makes an obscure request about the ill-fortune (முகடி) of mingling with them. The praise names Murugan the great treasure of Uma, the dark cuckoo of the Himalaya and green parrot whom Sankara loves, and the child who comes on the peacock with jingling bells, at the sea-washed courtyard of Senthil.
32.nuance: முகடியும் நலம் பிறந்திட அருள்வாயே: முகடி is the goddess of ill fortune (மூதேவி); the line may ask that even this ill fortune turn to good, or be divided otherwise. The praise centres on Uma (த்ரியம்பகி) more than on Murugan.

33.reading: The poet lists the courtesans' arts, loosening their hair, slipping their garments, looking from the corners of their eyes, asking for betel, laughing, calling 'come to our house', taking a man to bed and melting him while his wealth lasts, then, when it ends, beating him and driving him out if he enters; he asks when he will praise Murugan's feet and be rid of the blame of these one-sided unions. The praise is a long picture of the mountain stream in Valli's millet field, and names Murugan the life of Senthil, who gave the shastras to Siva with the crescent in his hair, the lord of ascetics.
33.nuance: ஒருதலை மருவு புணர்ச்சித் தூர்த்தர்கள்: the classical term for one-sided love is turned on the courtesan's bed, where only one side loves. வருபொருள் அளவில் ... வனைமனை புகுதில் அடித்துப் போக்கவும்: love lasting exactly as long as the money is the stock charge against courtesans. One word in the praise (மண்டுநநருர்) is garbled.

34.reading: The poet pictures the women once desired as they age: hair dark as a rain cloud turns grey like cotton, the spear-like eyes gather rheum like curdled sour curd and smell of flesh, the breasts that rivalled an elephant's temples become skin; he asks whether, understanding the state of women whose beauty perishes, he will not think of servanthood at Murugan's feet. The praise shows Brahma, Vishnu, Siva and Indra bowing to Murugan, who drank the milk-nectar from the breast of the Mother of all worlds, at Senthil where the conches roll in on the waves.
34.nuance: The argument against desire is decay rather than deceit: each charm is matched to its ruin (ஓதி நரை பஞ்சுபோல், விழி பீளை, கொங்கை தோல்). The plea names the remedy as வழியடிமை, hereditary servitude to the feet.

35.reading: The poet asks whether he will set his desire on women who talk tenderly, snatch coins, rage with rolling eyes, carry great blame, wound like serpents and measure the heart by the coin; he asks Murugan to rule him sweetly each day by grace, as one who calls his devotees with gracious eyes and talks with them. The praise names Siva who wears the aththi flower as his father, Vishnu the red light of the world whom ascetics and Vedic priests praise as his uncle, and the lord at Thiruchendur of rice fields, cane groves and plantains.
35.nuance: காசளவே மனம் உறைக்கும் தூரிகள்: their hearts are weighed exactly to the coin. The plea pictures the Lord's grace as intimacy, calling devotees and talking with them (அழைத்துஞ் சேதிகள் பேசிய).

links.note: Both hear the funeral drum over the corpse while kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still marries and seeks joy; 23 draws a different lesson, that one should share even a grain before the summons comes.
The Kural makes sharing one's food the chief of all duties; 23 arrives at the same act, sharing even a millet grain, through fear of death rather than compassion.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as a man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and in 33 the woman who melted him while wealth lasted beats him from the door when it ends.

Both turn desire away by showing the desired woman old. The Naladiyar gives one picture, the woman bent on her mother's staff; 34 takes each charm the songs praise, hair, eyes, breasts, and shows its ruin, then names a different remedy, service at the Lord's feet.
Both see the living body as a stinking corpse: the Naladiyar's cart torn by vultures once its axle breaks, and 30's body that already stinks, rots and rattles with worms and bones.
Both pray at the hour of death: 8 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's men strike, 28 that Death not call him while his body fails and his mother weeps, and that he reach the feet.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness deepens; the Kural's woman says it bewilders the whole town, while in 24 a mother names the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird as what wears her daughter down.

Thiruppugazh 21 gives the courtesans' own street talk: what you gave before is not enough, give today, come to my house (பண்டு தந்தது போதாதோ மேல் இன்று தந்து ... இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே வாரீர்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song stages exactly the இன்சொல் the Kural warns of, and lets the demand for money show through it.

Thiruppugazh 22 asks for the day when his mind loosens and dissolves, his speech ends and his own action perishes (சிந்தையும் அவிழ்ந்து அழிந்து உரையொழித்து என்செயல் அழிந்து) so that he sees Murugan. Tirumanthiram 1896 says silence is speech and mind both stilled, and that speech alone falling silent is mere muteness (வாக்கு மனமும் இரண்டும் மவுனமாம் ... மூங்கையாம்). The song asks for the end of mind as well as speech, which is the silence the Tirumanthiram counts as true.

Thiruppugazh 23 draws from the picture of Death's summons one remedy: without the delusion 'this is ours', share even half a kunri seed or a grain of millet, not putting it off to today or that day (எமதுபொருள் எனுமருளை இன்றி ... பங்கிட்டு உண்கை ... இன்றைக்கு அன்றைக்கு என நாடாது). Tirumanthiram 250 gives the same rule as commands: give to all without saying this one or that one, look out for others before eating, do not hoard old goods (ஆர்க்கும் இடுமின் அவரிவர் என்னன்மின் ... பழம்பொருள் போற்றன்மின்). The song supplies the reason the Tirumanthiram leaves unstated: the hour of death makes 'ours' a delusion.

Thiruppugazh 25, after calling his bathing in women's play an abhisheka, asks that he be given fine words in his heart to sing Murugan's paired feet and live (உன் இணையடிகள் பாடி வாழ எனெஞ்சில் செஞ்சொல் தருவாயே). Thiruppugazh 2 says he will not forget the grace by which Murugan told him to sing the Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழ் விருப்பமொடு செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை மறவேனே). The plea in 25 asks for the gift that the book's opening song says was given: song as the way out of the life it confesses.

Thiruppugazh 26 asks not to end in the false play of women's embraces but to think on the feet with birth ended, and its praise tells of the one who conquered with fire the Kama whose flower arrows frightened even ascetics (துறவினரும் தோற்று அஞ்சத் தனிமலர் அஞ்சு ஆர் புங்கத்து அமராடி ... தழலெழ வென்றார்). Tirumanthiram 346 reads the burning of Kama at Korukkai as inner restraint: settling the mind and destroying Kama's work is the yoga of tapas (காமன் செயலழித்து அங்கண் அருந்தவ யோகம்). Paired, the myth in the song's praise answers its plea: the conquest of Kama is the discipline the poet asks for. The reading of the praise is tentative.

Thiruppugazh 27 asks to see clearly how to leave the embrace of women (மகளிர் தோதக இன்பின் முயங்குதல் ஒழியுமாறு தெளிந்து) and to be given the feet held in mind by those who melt in the jnana of Sivayoga (சிவயோகத்து உருகு ஞான பரம்பர தந்திர அறிவினோர்). Tirumanthiram 831 says that only those who have reached the five-nazhigai paryanka yoga may embrace the woman with sandal on her breasts (பரியங்க யோகத்துப் பஞ்ச கடிகை ... அடைந்தவர்க்கு அல்லது ... தழுவ ஒருவற்கு ஒண்ணாதே). On the reading that the Tirumanthiram makes union itself a yoga for the adept, the two disagree about whether the yogi's path leaves the embrace or masters it.

Thiruppugazh 28 asks that Death not call him while his mind fails, speech goes and eyes roll (அறிவழிய மயல்பெருக உரையும் அற விழிசுழல), and asks now for the boon of drawing near the feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both fix the moment when speech is lost as the deadline; the Kural asks for good deeds before it, the song for the Lord's feet.

Thiruppugazh 29 asks whether he will gain grace if Murugan calls him and gives him his sandals (விளித்து உன் பாதுகை நீதர நானருள் பெறுவேனோ), just after naming Rama, the uncle, in the praise. Thiruppugazh 1187, after a funeral, asks to be set holding Murugan's two sandals (இருபாதுகையைப் பற்றி நிற்க வைத்தெனை அருளாதோ). Only these two songs ask for the sandals rather than the feet, a humbler refuge; in 29 the image may borrow from the sandals Rama left as a sign of rule.

Thiruppugazh 31 asks not to wander night and day thinking of a woman but to bathe in the sea of Murugan's compassion and be given the love that knows him within (உனை எனதுள் அறியும் அன்பைத் தருவாயே). Tirumanthiram 270 says love and Siva are not two, and that those who know it rest as love that is Siva (அன்பே சிவமாய் அமர்ந்திருந்தாரே). The song asks for love as the means of knowing the Lord inside; the Tirumanthiram takes the step further and makes the love and the Lord one.

Thiruppugazh 32, after describing lovemaking with women scented with sandal and kumkum, asks about the முகடி, the goddess of ill fortune, of mingling with them (அரிவையருடன் கலந்திடு முகடியும் நலம்பிறந்திட அருள்வாயே). Kural 936 calls gambling a முகடி that covers those it swallows (சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார்). Both name a vice as the ill-fortune goddess herself; Kural 920 already sets women, liquor and dice together. The sense of the song's line is uncertain.

Thiruppugazh 33 calls the courtesan's bed a one-sided union (ஒருதலை மருவு புணர்ச்சித் தூர்த்தர்கள்), where she melts a man only while his wealth lasts. Kural 1196, in a woman's voice, says love is painful on one side only and sweet on both, like the load of a carrying pole (ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம் காப்போல இருதலையானும் இனிது). The song takes the akam term for unreturned longing and turns it on paid love, where only the man loves.

Thiruppugazh 35 speaks of women who talk tenderly, snatch coins and whose hearts are weighed exactly to the coin (உருக்கம் பேசிய நீலியர் ... காசளவே மனம் உறைக்கும் தூரிகள்). Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the gain and then speak of their goodness (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்). Both describe the same weighing, tender speech measured by the money.

source_issues: Song 21: two corrupt characters, in வா஡ண (line 10, probably வாரீ, 'come') and வானு஡ (line 13, probably வானூடு); also the unflagged garble நநடுர் கேர்டுர் in line 22.
Song 33: unflagged garble மண்டுநநருர் (line 15); the source seems to use நந for a lost letter here and in 21.
